emails.subject: the note she kept for six years
emails.preview_text: A sticky note. Six years. Here’s why it mattered.
emails.body_text:
A friend of mine found a sticky note in an old jacket pocket last week. Three words from a coworker, written six years ago: ‘you’ve got this.’

She stood in her closet and cried. Not because she was sad — because in a hard week, those three words from six years ago still knew exactly what to say.

Your words have a longer shelf life than you think. Go put some out there.

emails.subject: he sent 52 cards in a year
emails.preview_text: One card every Sunday. Here’s what happened.
emails.body_text:
Last year, a guy decided to send one encouragement card every Sunday. Fifty-two cards. Friends, family, his mail carrier.

By December, three different people told him his card arrived on the worst day of their year. He had no idea. He was just being consistent.

You don’t have to send 52. One is a fine place to start.

emails.subject: what the barista wrote on the cup
emails.preview_text: Four words on a coffee cup changed her morning.
emails.body_text:
A woman was having the worst Thursday. Then her coffee cup came back with four words on it: ‘you’re doing great, mama.’

She doesn’t know the barista’s name. She’ll probably never see them again. But she told that story to everyone she knows, because it rewired her whole day.

Kindness doesn’t need a reason or a relationship. Just a moment.

emails.subject: the voicemail he saved for a decade
emails.preview_text: He kept one voicemail for ten years. Here’s why.
emails.body_text:
A man kept the same voicemail on his phone for ten years. Just his dad saying ‘proud of you, son. Call when you can.’

His dad’s been gone for six of those years. That forty-second message became the most valuable thing he owns.

Tell people you’re proud of them while they can hear it. Leave the voicemail. Send the card.
